title: The Agent-Ready Score: 16 Questions That Tell You If Your AI Ops Tool Survives Day 30
subtitle: A readiness diagnostic for $1-10M service firm owners and ops leads building or running internal AI ops tools. Score one process across the 5 things that decide whether the tool lives or dies.

methodology_anchor.name: Agent-Ready Ops
preconditions: Structured input data. Your data sources are clean enough to be the input layer for an automated decision.
Documentable decision logic. The rules a human follows can be written down explicitly.
Narrow initial scope. The first cut handles a single decision in a single workflow, not a sweep.
Human-in-the-loop by design. Every output touches a person before it ships externally.
methodology_anchor.intro: This assessment scores against the four preconditions for Agent-Ready Ops, plus the process visibility that sits underneath them. Hit all four and the process can carry an AI tool. Miss one and any build will leak.

proof_card.sample_top_leak: free-text intake scattered across 5 systems (~9 hrs/week recoverable)

answers.label: Solo or 2 to 5 people, under $1M revenue
$1M to $3M, around 6 to 20 people
$3M to $6M, around 20 to 50 people
$6M to $10M and up, 50 to 100 people

start_screen.headline_html: See whether the process you want to automate can carry an AI tool.
start_screen.description: For $1-10M service firm owners and ops leads. Sixteen questions about the one process you most want to automate, then a 0 to 100 score and the first thing to fix before you build.

questions.text: How completely have you mapped this process from trigger to finish?

answers.label: 1. Never written down, it just happens
2. A rough version lives in my head
3. Partial doc covering the main path
4. Documented end to end, missing a few edge cases
5. Full map: every step, every handoff, who touches what

questions.text: How well do you know the weekly hours this process costs your team?

answers.label: 1. No idea
2. A loose guess
3. I could estimate within a couple hours
4. I've counted it once
5. I track it and the number is current

questions.text: When the person who owns this process is out, what happens?

answers.label: 1. It stops or breaks
2. It limps along and quality drops
3. It slows down but survives
4. Someone covers it from memory
5. Anyone can run it straight from a doc

questions.text: How clearly can you name where this process leaks time today?

answers.label: 1. I've never looked
2. I have a hunch
3. I know the rough area
4. I've found the main bottleneck
5. I've quantified each leak point

low.headline: You're flying blind on this process
low.text: You can't automate a path you've never walked end to end. Right now the steps live in someone's head, so any AI tool you build automates a guess. Map it first.
steps: Write the process out step by step, trigger to finish
Note who touches each step and what they do
Time one full run so you know the weekly hours at stake

mid.headline: You see the shape, not the leaks
mid.text: You know roughly how this runs, but the bottleneck and the real hours aren't pinned down. That gap is where an AI tool quietly breaks. Tighten the map before you build.
steps: Turn your mental model into a written doc
Mark the single step that eats the most time
Confirm someone else could run it from your doc

high.headline: The process is visible. Keep it that way.
high.text: You've mapped it and you know the numbers. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Version the process doc so it stays current
Track weekly hours over time to catch drift
Pre-write the edge cases that still need a judgment call

operator_brief.headline_number: ~9 hrs/week hidden in this one process
operator_brief.lever: My read: write the process down before you write a single automation, the doc is the build spec.
talking_points: This process costs us roughly a full day of team time every week.
If the owner is out, we either stop or redo the work.
We can't price an AI build until we've mapped what it replaces.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Shadow one full run this week, write each step as it happens, then time it.

questions.text: What does the data going into this process look like?

answers.label: 1. Emails, DMs, and whatever the client sends
2. Mostly free text with a little structure
3. A mix of forms and free text
4. Forms with a few optional fields
5. Structured fields with required answers

questions.text: How consolidated is the intake for this process?

answers.label: 1. Scattered across email, Slack, calls, and docs
2. A few main places, no single source
3. Mostly one place, with regular exceptions
4. One system, occasional side channels
5. One form or system everyone uses

questions.text: How many separate systems hold the information this process needs?

answers.label: 1. Five or more
2. Four
3. Three
4. Two
5. One

low.headline: Messy in, faster mess out
low.text: Your intake is free text spread across systems, so a model gets messy input and hands you messy output quicker. The fix sits upstream, in how the data arrives.
steps: Replace free-text intake with a structured form
Make the fields that matter required, not optional
Pick one system as the single front door

mid.headline: Half-structured intake, half the reliability
mid.text: Some of this arrives in forms, some is whatever the client sends. The free-text slice is where the tool trips. Close that gap before you build.
steps: Audit which fields still come in as free text
Convert the high-value ones to structured inputs
Cut the number of systems holding this data

high.headline: Clean inputs. Build on them.
high.text: Structured, consolidated intake means a tool reads exactly what it needs. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add validation so bad input never enters
Auto-route intake into the systems that need it
Hold the source count to one or two

operator_brief.headline_number: data spread across 3+ systems per run
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: collapse intake to one structured form before touching any AI.
talking_points: Right now the same info gets entered more than once across tools.
Free-text intake is why outputs need so much cleanup.
One clean front door cuts errors before the tool ever runs.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Build one structured intake form for this process and route a week of real requests through it.

questions.text: How well can your best person explain the rules they follow here?

answers.label: 1. It's pure judgment, can't be explained
2. They know it but can't put it in words
3. They can explain the common cases
4. Most rules are written, judgment fills the gaps
5. The decision rules are fully documented

questions.text: How consistent is the outcome when two people run this process?

answers.label: 1. Totally different results
2. Noticeably different
3. Similar, with personal quirks
4. Nearly identical
5. Identical, the rules decide, not the person

questions.text: How clearly defined is "done" for this process?

answers.label: 1. We know it when we see it
2. Loosely, it varies by person
3. A shared idea, not written
4. A documented checklist most people follow
5. Explicit done criteria, checked every time

low.headline: The rules live in one person's gut
low.text: If your best person can't explain how they decide, you can't encode it. A tool needs explicit rules, and right now they're tacit. Get them on paper.
steps: Sit with the person who runs this and ask why at each decision
Write the rules they actually follow, not the ones on paper
Define what done looks like in plain terms

mid.headline: Rules exist, judgment still fills the gaps
mid.text: You can explain the common cases, but the edges still ride on instinct. Those edges are where outputs diverge. Pin them down before you automate.
steps: List the cases where two people would decide differently
Write rules for the most frequent of those
Document the done criteria as a checklist

high.headline: Documented logic. Encode it.
high.text: Your decision rules are written and outcomes are consistent. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Test the rules against a batch of past cases
Flag the rare cases that still need a human call
Keep the rule doc beside the build so it stays in sync

operator_brief.headline_number: ~20% of cases decided by gut, not rule
operator_brief.lever: Honest take: documentable decision logic is the precondition most firms skip and most builds die on.
talking_points: Two people run this process today and get different results.
The rules our best person uses have never been written down.
Without explicit rules, an AI tool guesses and we own the mistakes.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Have your best operator narrate ten real decisions out loud and capture the rule behind each.

questions.text: How predictable are the cases this process handles?

answers.label: 1. Almost every case is an exception
2. Exceptions are common
3. Roughly half follow a pattern
4. Most cases follow a clear pattern
5. 80%+ are predictable, edge cases are rare

questions.text: Could you carve off one slice of this to automate first?

answers.label: 1. No, it's all tangled together
2. Maybe, haven't thought about it
3. Possibly, with some untangling
4. Yes, I can see one clear slice
5. Already isolated the highest-value slice

questions.text: How tightly is this process scoped to a single decision or output?

answers.label: 1. It sprawls across many decisions
2. It covers several loosely related steps
3. A few connected decisions
4. Mostly one decision with a few branches
5. One decision, one output, clean boundary

low.headline: Too sprawling to automate safely
low.text: This process covers many decisions at once, so a first build breaks on edge case three. Narrow it to one slice before anything else.
steps: List every distinct decision this process makes
Pick the single highest-volume one
Scope the first build to that decision only

mid.headline: Close to a clean slice
mid.text: You can see where to cut, but the process still bundles a few jobs together. Isolate one before you build so the tool has a clear boundary.
steps: Separate the predictable cases from the exceptions
Define the one decision the tool will own
Route everything outside that scope to a person

high.headline: Tight scope. Ship narrow.
high.text: One decision, one output, a clean boundary. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Ship the narrow build and measure it for two weeks
Only widen scope once the first slice holds
Keep edge cases out of v1 on purpose

operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: build for the predictable 80% and route the rest to review, never the reverse.
talking_points: Most runs of this process are predictable, the exceptions are loud.
A narrow first build ships in weeks, a broad one stalls for months.
Edge cases belong with a human until the core proves itself.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Pick the single most repetitive decision in this process and scope a one-week build around just that.

questions.text: How clear is who reviews output before it ships externally?

answers.label: 1. Nobody reviews, it just goes out
2. Sometimes, depends who's around
3. Reviewed when someone remembers
4. A named person reviews most of it
5. Every external output has a named reviewer

questions.text: How ready are you to route uncertain cases to a human?

answers.label: 1. No fallback planned
2. We'd figure it out later
3. A rough idea of who would catch it
4. A defined path for exceptions
5. A built review queue with clear triggers

questions.text: How do you currently catch errors in this process?

answers.label: 1. We find out when a client complains
2. We catch some, miss some
3. A spot check now and then
4. A regular review catches most
5. A checkpoint catches errors before they ship

low.headline: No safety net on the output
low.text: Nothing reviews this before it goes out, so an AI tool ships its mistakes straight to clients. Build the review step before you build the tool.
steps: Name who reviews output before it leaves the building
Decide which cases must be checked by a human
Set a simple rule for what gets flagged

mid.headline: Review happens when someone remembers
mid.text: There's some checking, but it's inconsistent. Inconsistent review is how errors slip through once volume rises. Make the review path explicit.
steps: Assign a named reviewer for external output
Define the triggers that route a case to review
Track what the review actually catches

high.headline: Review is designed in. Good.
high.text: Every external output has a reviewer and a clear path for exceptions. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Tune the review queue so only uncertain cases hit it
Aim for 15-20% routed to a human by design
Log corrections to feed back into the rules

operator_brief.headline_number: 0 to 15-20% of cases should route to review
operator_brief.lever: My read: human-in-the-loop is design, not failure, so plan it from day one.
talking_points: Today errors surface when a client complains, which is the worst time.
A built review step catches mistakes before they ship.
Routing 15-20% to a person is what makes the other 80% safe to automate.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Add one review checkpoint to this process for a week and log every error it catches.
